442.title: Or — a luminous object; or a sorrowless mind; or a great heart (1.35–1.39)
442.hook: five more 'or's, ending with the most generous line in the Yoga Sutras: whatever you find dear
442.tomorrow: mastery from the smallest to the largest
442.howItsDone: Hindu meditators use many supports, from an inner light in the heart to the image of a saint or a chosen form of God, and teachers often cite sutra 1.39 to encourage each student to meditate on what is dear to them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: or, the breath. A long breath out, a small rest at the bottom. Today Patanjali keeps opening doors, five in a row.
screen: `OR THE BREATH — A LONG BREATH OUT.`

segments.voice: A big old house has a front door, a back door, a side gate, a door from the garage, and a window someone always climbs through. Everyone in the family gets in a different way, and nobody argues about which door is the real one. They just want to get home. In sutras 1.35 to 1.39, Patanjali becomes that house. Five more sutras, and each begins with the same word: or.
screen: `A HOUSE WITH MANY DOORS.` → `NOBODY ARGUES WHICH IS REAL.` → `FIVE MORE SUTRAS: OR.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.35: or, when a subtle sense experience arises, it holds the mind steady. The commentator Vyasa's example: resting attention on the tip of the nose, a practitioner may sense an unusually fine fragrance. The point isn't the fragrance. A vivid, fine sensation can anchor a wandering mind. Sutra 1.36: or, the sorrowless, luminous one. Vyasa places it in the heart, an inner light without grief; some teachers picture a soft light in the chest. Sutra 1.37: or, a mind that takes as its object someone free of attachment. A great heart, a saint, a teacher: Vyasa says a mind colored by one free of passion finds its footing. Sutra 1.38: or, resting on what's known in dream or in deep sleep: the stillness of dreamless sleep, or an inspiring dream, as a support. And sutra 1.39, short and wide open: or, by meditating on whatever you find dear. After all the talk of effort, the list leaves the choice to the practitioner. Not because anything goes. Vyasa explains: once the mind finds its footing on what it likes, it can find its footing elsewhere too. The whole sweep, from 1.33 to 1.39: four attitudes, the breath, a fine sensation, an inner light, a great heart, dream and sleep, anything dear. Many doors. One house.

segments.voice: Today you choose the door: a soft light in the chest, the face of someone whose goodness you trust, an image you love like the sea or a flame, or, if you pray, a form of God dear to you. Rest your attention there. When the mind wanders, come back through the same door.
Or. Five more times in sutras 1.35 to 1.39: a fine sensation, an inner light, a great heart, dream and sleep, and whatever you find dear.
Your line: many doors. Whichever one you use, it opens into the same house. Until tomorrow.

443.title: Mastery from the smallest to the largest (1.40)
443.hook: a mind steadied through any of the doors can rest on anything, from a speck to the sky
443.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras treat 1.40 as the sign that the mind has been steadied, and teachers then move to the crystal image of 1.41 to describe what deeper absorption is like.

segments.voice: Yesterday: many doors, ending with whatever you find dear. Today, what's waiting once you're through.

A good photographer can focus on a grain of pollen on a bee's leg, then pull back and frame a mountain range at dusk, without changing cameras. The size of the thing doesn't matter. The lens holds steady on whatever it's pointed at. Patanjali has spent seven sutras offering doors into a steady mind. Sutra 1.40 says what a mind like that can hold, at both ends of the scale.
screen: `POLLEN ON A BEE'S LEG.` → `A MOUNTAIN RANGE AT DUSK.` → `ONE STEADY LENS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.40, in paraphrase: the yogi's mastery extends from the smallest particle to the greatest magnitude. Paramanu, the smallest atom. Parama mahat, the greatest greatness. Vashikara, mastery, having it under one's control. What kind of mastery? The commentator Vyasa explains that the mind can now settle on the subtlest object without slipping, and on the vastest without losing its grip. Small doesn't make it fidget. Huge doesn't make it scatter. You may hear an echo of the Shvetashvatara, a little over two weeks ago: smaller than small, greater than great. There the words described the self. Here they describe the reach of a steadied mind. The sutra is also a hinge. The long list of doors is finished, and from here Patanjali turns to what happens inside absorption itself. The next sutra brings one more image, a mind like a clear crystal, and that's where today's line comes from. Tomorrow unfolds it. For today, the direction is enough: a mind steadied through any door becomes clear enough to hold anything, from a speck of dust to the whole sky.

segments.voice: Rest your attention on the smallest thing you can feel, a fingertip on your knee, then widen to the whole body, the room, the sky above the roof, and come back to the fingertip. Small, then large, then small. The aim isn't to see far, only to notice whether the steadiness holds as the size changes.
Vashikara, mastery, having it under control. Sutra 1.40: a steadied mind can rest on anything, from the tiniest particle to the greatest expanse.
Your line: the clear crystal. Tomorrow you'll see what it does with color. Day four hundred forty-three, done.

444.title: The stages of absorption (1.41–1.46)
444.hook: a clear crystal on a red cloth looks red; Patanjali says a still mind behaves the same way
444.howItsDone: Teachers of classical yoga describe samapatti as the mind becoming transparent to its object, and they guide students from coarse objects, such as an image or the breath, toward subtler ones over long practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vashikara, mastery from the smallest to the largest, and a hint of a clear crystal. Today, the crystal itself.

Put a clear glass bead on a red cloth. It looks red. Slide it onto blue silk: blue. Set it on a leaf, and it glows green. The bead hasn't changed at all. It has no color of its own, and that's exactly why it can show every color perfectly. Much of the time a mind isn't like that. It's tinted glass: everything it looks at comes back colored with worry, wanting, labels. Sutra 1.41 describes the moment the tint drains away.
screen: `A CLEAR BEAD ON RED CLOTH.` → `ON BLUE SILK. ON A LEAF.` → `NO COLOR OF ITS OWN.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.41, in paraphrase: when the turnings have dwindled, the mind becomes like a fine, transparent jewel, and takes on the form of whatever it rests on, whether the knower, the act of knowing, or the thing known. That merging is samapatti, coinciding. The crystal takes the color. Then Patanjali lays out the stages. First, savitarka: absorption on a coarse object, still mixed with three things, the word, the object, and the idea of it. Vyasa's example is a cow: the sound cow, the animal, and the thought of a cow, all tangled together. Next, nirvitarka. Memory is cleaned out, the mind becomes as if empty of its own form, and only the object shines. Not the label cow. Just the cow, seen. Sutra 1.44 says the same two steps happen with subtle objects: savichara, still with some thinking, and nirvichara, without it. Sutra 1.45 says subtle objects go all the way back to the unmanifest, the root of nature itself. And 1.46 gathers the set: these are samadhi with seed, the phrase you met ten days ago. Now you know what the seeds are: every object, coarse or subtle, that the clear mind still rests on. The first step is the practical one. Much of the time, people see names, not things. The crystal begins when the name drops away for a moment, and the thing itself is simply there.

segments.voice: Look at an object near you, a cup, a plant, your own hand, and notice the name arrive, then the ideas: mine, chipped, needs washing. Gently let them go and just look: shape, light, color. Then close your eyes and hold the object in mind without words, like the crystal on the cloth.
Samapatti, coinciding, the mind taking the form of what it rests on. The stages move from thought to without, on coarse objects and on subtle ones, the steps of samadhi with seed.
Your line: the crystal takes the color. A clear mind adds no tint of its own. See you tomorrow.

445.title: Truth-bearing wisdom (1.47–1.50)
445.hook: at the clearest stage of absorption, Patanjali says a different kind of knowing appears, and gives it an old Vedic name
445.howItsDone: In classical yoga, ritambhara prajna is described as the fruit of mature absorption, and teachers often contrast it with book learning and reasoning, both valued as steps along the way.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samapatti, the crystal takes the color, with labels and then without, on coarse objects and then subtle ones. Today, what the clearest crystal knows.

There are two ways to know your grandmother's kitchen. You can read a description of it: yellow walls, a table by the window, a smell of cardamom. Or you can stand in it. Both are real knowledge. But only one knows this kitchen, this light on this afternoon, this exact chipped cup. Patanjali says that at the clearest stage of absorption, the mind stops knowing about things and starts knowing them, one by one, as they are.
screen: `A DESCRIPTION OF THE KITCHEN.` → `STANDING IN IT.` → `KNOWING ABOUT, AND KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.47: when nirvichara, the subtle absorption without thinking, becomes fully clear and skillful, there is inner serenity: adhyatma prasada, the self made calm and bright. Sutra 1.48: there, wisdom is ritambhara. Truth-bearing. Ritam is a very old word. In the Rig Veda, rita is the cosmic order, the rightness that makes the sun rise and the seasons turn, closely tied to truth itself. Bhara means bearing, full of. So ritambhara is wisdom that carries the truth in it, wisdom that can't be mistaken, because nothing of the mind's own color has been added. Sutra 1.49 says how it differs from ordinary knowledge. What you learn by testimony, from a teacher or a book, and by inference, reasoning it out, is about things in general. Truth-bearing wisdom has a different object: the particular. Not what kitchens are like. This kitchen. Not what a self is. This one, here. And sutra 1.50 adds something subtle. Every experience leaves an impression, a samskara, a groove in the mind. The impression left by this wisdom is so strong that it blocks the others, like a deep, clean groove the water now runs in, so the old ruts dry up. That's why, for Patanjali, this isn't the end yet. One impression is left: this wisdom's own. Tomorrow, he says what happens when even that is let go.

Truth-bearing wisdom. Ritambhara prajna, sutra 1.48: the knowing that arises in the clearest absorption, full of truth, and aimed at the particular, as it is.
Your line: ritambhara. Wisdom that knows this one, here, as it is. That's day four hundred forty-five.

446.title: Seedless (1.51)
446.hook: the first chapter of the Yoga Sutras ends by letting go of the very last thing the mind holds
446.howItsDone: In classical yoga, seedless samadhi is described as the culmination of practice, and students study the whole first chapter as a map from the definition of yoga in 1.2 to its completion in 1.51.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ritambhara, truth-bearing wisdom, the knowing that carries the truth and leaves a groove that blocks all the others. Today, the last sutra of chapter one.

A gardener clears a field. First the big weeds. Then the small ones. Then the seeds still lying in the soil, waiting to sprout. At last one seed is left: the special one she planted on purpose, the one that crowded out the weeds. The field is quiet and clean. And now, strangely, she lets that one go too. Not because it was bad. Because the field was the point all along. That's sutra 1.51, the last line of the first chapter.
screen: `THE BIG WEEDS, THE SMALL ONES.` → `ONE GOOD SEED LEFT.` → `SHE LETS THAT ONE GO TOO.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.51: tasyapi nirodhe sarva nirodhan nirbijah samadhih. When even that is stilled, everything being stilled, there is seedless absorption. Even that: the impression left by yesterday's truth-bearing wisdom, the last good groove in the mind. When it too goes quiet, nothing is left that could sprout again. Nirbija: without seed. Vyasa explains that the mind then dissolves back into its source, and the seer, purusha, rests alone, pure and free. That loops back to the third sutra, fifteen days ago: then the seer rests in its own form. The first chapter is a circle. It began with the definition of yoga, and it ends with yoga complete. Look at the path it walked. Atha, now. The seer. The five turnings. Practice and non-attachment. Samadhi with seed, and without. The born-free and the rest of us. Or, devotion to Ishvara. Om, repeated with its meaning. The nine obstacles. One thing. The four keys. Or the breath. Many doors. Mastery, small to large. The crystal taking the color. Truth-bearing wisdom. And seedless. Seventeen sessions, from now to nothing held. This chapter is the Samadhi Pada, the part on absorption. Tomorrow begins the Sadhana Pada, the part on practice, and it starts with three simple things.

447.title: Kriya yoga — discipline, study, surrender (2.1–2.2)
447.hook: the second chapter of the Yoga Sutras opens for busy, scattered minds with a three-part yoga of action
447.howItsDone: Some Hindus who follow the Yoga Sutras practice kriya yoga as a daily rhythm: a disciplined habit such as early rising or fasting, regular study of scripture or mantra repetition, and offering the day's actions to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nirbija, seedless, the end of chapter one, where even the last good seed is let go. Today, chapter two begins.

Chapter one was beautiful: stilling the mind, the clear crystal, seedless absorption. It can also sound like a story about astronauts, wonderful and a long way from a job, a family, a buzzing phone and a mind with forty tabs open. The commentator Vyasa seems to have expected that. The first chapter, he says, speaks to a mind already settled. The second is for a mind that is still scattered. And it opens with something you can do this afternoon.
screen: `CHAPTER ONE: THE ASTRONAUTS.` → `A MIND WITH FORTY TABS.` → `CHAPTER TWO: FOR THE REST OF US.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.1: tapah svadhyaya ishvara pranidhanani kriya yogah. Discipline, study and surrender to the Lord are the yoga of action. Kriya means action, doing: yoga you do in daily life, before the deep stillness comes. Three parts. Tapas, discipline, literally heat, the warmth of effort. Vyasa insists it shouldn't wreck your health; it's the steady heat of keeping your commitments when comfort pulls the other way. Svadhyaya, study, literally one's own reading: study of the sacred texts, and Vyasa adds repetition of om or a mantra. Some modern teachers also hear study of oneself in it. Ishvara pranidhana, surrender to the Lord, which chapter one offered as a shortcut. Here Vyasa reads it as offering all your actions to the Lord, the supreme teacher, and letting go of their fruits. Sutra 2.2 says why: to cultivate samadhi, and to thin the afflictions. Thinning is the key word. Not destroying them in one blow. Wearing them down, the way water wears down stone. The three balance each other. Discipline is effort, study is understanding, surrender is letting go: body, mind, heart. Only discipline, and you'd turn rigid. Only study, and you'd turn clever. Only surrender, and you might drift. Together they make a practice an ordinary person can live. The same three return later in this chapter, as the last three of the five observances.

segments.voice: Try all three in miniature: sit still for a few breaths, even when the body wants to shift; notice honestly, as if reading a page, how your mind is right now, restless, tired or calm; then offer this sit to something greater, God if you pray, or simply let go of needing it to be good. Then rest on the breath.
Kriya yoga. The yoga of action in sutra 2.1: discipline, study and surrender to the Lord, practiced to cultivate absorption and thin the afflictions.
Your line: three. Effort, understanding and letting go, held together in one practice. Until tomorrow.

448.title: The five afflictions (2.3)
448.hook: one short sutra names the five roots of human trouble, in the order they grow
448.tomorrow: ignorance — mistaking the passing for the permanent
448.howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras learn the five kleshas as the root diagnosis of suffering, and some teachers ask them to trace everyday reactions back to these roots during meditation and daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kriya yoga. Three: discipline, study and surrender, to cultivate absorption and thin the afflictions. Today, what exactly gets thinned, and the week closes.

A doctor can treat a fever, or find the infection causing it. It's easy to spend a life treating fevers: a flash of anger here, a craving there, a wave of fear at 2am. Patanjali goes looking for the infection. In sutra 2.3 he names the afflictions. There are five, and the commentators read their order as a line of growth, each one coming out of the one before, like branches from a trunk.
screen: `TREATING THE FEVER.` → `FINDING THE INFECTION.` → `FIVE ROOTS, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Sutra 2.3: avidya asmita raga dvesha abhiniveshah kleshah. Ignorance, I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life are the afflictions. Klesha means affliction, something that causes pain. Here's the order, quickly, since each gets its own day. Avidya, ignorance: not a lack of facts, but seeing wrongly, taking what passes for what lasts. Asmita, I-ness: the sense of a separate me that grows out of that mistake. Raga, attraction: the pull toward what pleased that me. Dvesha, aversion: the push away from what hurt it. Abhinivesha, clinging to life: the deep fear of ending, which Patanjali says is found even in the wise. The commentators read it as a family tree. Misreading reality produces a small, separate self. A separate self wants things and fears things. And under all the wanting and fearing runs the will to keep going at any cost. What isn't on the list: no demons, no sins, no bad luck. Just five ways the mind gets reality wrong and then defends the mistake. Now the week, from the top. Day one, many doors. Day two, mastery from the smallest to the largest. Day three, the crystal takes the color. Day four, truth-bearing wisdom. Day five, seedless, the end of chapter one. Day six, kriya yoga, chapter two begins. Today, the five afflictions, the roots the whole practice is meant to thin.
screen: `KLESHA: AN AFFLICTION.` · `IGNORANCE, THEN I-NESS.` · `ATTRACTION, AVERSION, CLINGING.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `FIVE ROOTS, ONE FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: As thoughts come, sort them gently into the five: wanting something is attraction, avoiding something is aversion, me and my image is I-ness, a flicker of fear about the future is clinging. You don't need to find ignorance; it's said to be under all of them. Just notice, name, and return to the breath.

Avidya, ignorance, mistaking the passing for the lasting, the root of the five afflictions. Patanjali names it first, then I-ness, attraction, aversion and clinging to life, each growing from the one before.
Your line: kleshas. No demons, no bad luck: five ways of getting reality wrong. That's the week.
